title: GitHub Reference
description: A quick reminder of the ideas and examples in the GitHub lessons. Open the linked lesson when you need more help.

entries.name: Git and GitHub have different jobs
entries.summary: Git records file history on a computer. GitHub hosts Git repositories and adds pages for collaboration. You can learn local Git without a GitHub account.

example.code:
Local computer: edit files and record Git commits
GitHub repository: share selected commits and review proposed changes

notes: Do not confuse an account on a hosting service with local version history.

entries.name: Find your way around a repository
entries.summary: A GitHub repository page has areas for code and collaboration. Start with its README, then inspect the files and recent changes.

example.code:
Code: files and README
Issues: problems and ideas
Pull requests: proposed code changes
Actions: configured automated runs

notes: A public repository can still contain code that is unsafe to run; read setup steps before using them.

entries.name: Follow the GitHub Flow
entries.summary: GitHub Flow is a lightweight way to work on changes. A focused branch and pull request let people inspect an idea before it joins the main branch.

example.code: Create a branch -> make focused commits -> open a pull request -> review and check -> merge when ready

notes: Do not combine unrelated unfinished features into one small review.

entries.name: Write an issue someone can reproduce
entries.summary: A GitHub issue can record a bug or proposed task. A useful bug report gives steps, expected behaviour and actual behaviour.

example.code:
Title: Search misses lowercase moon
Steps: type moon in the book search
Expected: Moon appears
Actual: no matching book appears

notes: Never put passwords or private learner records into a public issue.

entries.name: Explain a pull request
entries.summary: A pull request, often called a PR, proposes combining changes from one branch into another. Its description should explain the result for a reviewer.

example.code:
Base branch: main
Head branch: fix-search-case
Problem: lowercase queries missed titles
Change: compare title and query in lowercase
Check: Moon and moon both match

notes: Opening a PR does not mean it has been approved or merged.

entries.name: Use the Files changed view
entries.summary: The Files changed view shows the difference a PR proposes. Review the actual lines and ask focused questions about behaviour and edge cases.

example.code:
Old: title === query
New: title.toLowerCase() === query.toLowerCase()
Review question: should outside spaces also be ignored?

notes: A small diff can still change important behaviour; read it instead of judging only its size.

entries.name: Understand review outcomes
entries.summary: A GitHub review may comment, approve or request changes. Project branch rules determine which reviews are required before merging.

example.code:
Comment: asks a question or gives feedback
Approve: reviewer considers the change ready
Request changes: reviewer identifies work needed

notes: Resolve the reason for a review request; do not just hide its comment.

entries.name: Read an Actions check
entries.summary: GitHub Actions can run a workflow when code changes. A workflow is a configured set of jobs and steps. Its check reports whether those steps succeeded.

example.code:
Workflow file: .github/workflows/check.yml
Job: test
Step: run the project test command
Result: passed

notes: Read logs and configuration before relying on a badge whose checks you do not know.

entries.name: Protect the main branch with rules
entries.summary: Repository rules can require reviews or status checks before a branch accepts changes. This helps a team apply the same process consistently.

example.code:
Worked rule plan for main:
Require a pull request
Require the test status check
Require a suitable review
Allow only intended people to bypass rules

notes: A rule only helps when it is configured for the intended branch and used consistently.

entries.name: Fork a project or clone it
entries.summary: A fork is a hosted repository linked to an upstream project. A clone is a local repository copy. A fork can hold proposed contributions without granting write access to upstream.

example.code:
Upstream project -> your hosted fork
Hosted fork -> local clone
Local commits -> proposed change from the fork

notes: Forking does not remove the original licence or give permission for every use.

entries.name: Explain a version with a release
entries.summary: A Git tag names a specific point in history. A GitHub release can add notes and downloadable files around a tag.

example.code:
Tag: v1.1.0
Release title: Search improvement
Notes: search now ignores letter case
Known limit: outside spaces are still significant

notes: Do not claim a release fixes all bugs when only one behaviour changed.

entries.name: Read the community files
entries.summary: Community files help people use and contribute to a repository. A licence explains reuse conditions; other files describe participation and reporting.

example.code:
README.md: purpose and setup
LICENSE: reuse conditions
CONTRIBUTING.md: how to propose a change
CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md: community behaviour
SECURITY.md: how to report a security issue if provided

notes: Public visibility alone does not mean code has no reuse conditions.
